extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Civil War history; military officers and newspaper editors interested in wartime occupation practices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observed practices for managing, censoring, and directing local newspapers and trade in a city captured during wartime, plus associated military/press conduct and operational lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military appointment to take charge of editorial department
rubrics_metrics.description: When military authorities deem it necessary, they may appoint northern/loyal editors to 'take charge of the editorial department' of a captured paper while leaving business management to the proprietors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in General Wallace's order: appoint experienced editors 'to take charge of the editorial department' and 'the business management of your office will be left to you.' Publish the order publicly and expect owners to issue disclaimers of editorial responsibility while under the order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit supervision to editorial content; do not close business operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference should be limited to the editorial voice: 'the business management and the general miscellaneous and news matter were not interfered with.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervisors should focus on controlling/opining content while allowing the paper's business and non-editorial reporting to continue, reducing economic harm and friction with proprietors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial messaging under occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors placed in charge should 'plainly announce the determination of the Government to assert itself and put down and punish treason' and insist that Union armies have 'entered Memphis ... to stay there' while 'crediting the Rebels with much bravery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a positive, authoritative tone: assert government authority, warn about the harms of partisan/guerrilla warfare, discourage resistance as futile, yet acknowledge opponent bravery to preserve credibility and avoid needlessly inflaming readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about the change in editorial control
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers may print the military order at the head of the columns and explicitly state they are 'not responsible for any thing which should appear editorially, as long as the order was in force.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editorial control is externally imposed, make the arrangement visible to readers and allow proprietors to disclaim responsibility to reduce misunderstanding and legal/ethical disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove supervision when alternative loyal press is established
rubrics_metrics.description: General Wallace 'assured its proprietors that he should remove the editorial supervision as soon as a Union paper was established in Memphis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use temporary supervisory measures: restore original management once a loyal press organ can be sustained to respect promises and minimize long-term occupation interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing sincerity of claimed loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: The text distinguishes genuine loyalty from opportunistic conversions: 'There were many men ... ready ... to swear allegiance to the victorious side, who joined our standard because they considered the Rebel cause a losing one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate loyalty by prior conduct (acceptance of office under Rebels, past acts) rather than merely by recent declarations; be wary of 'newly converted loyalist' seeking favors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using visible local behavior to gauge popular sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical signs of loyalty included physical acts at landing: 'As their mooring-lines were thrown on shore they were seized by dozens of persons in the crowd' — evidence that the laboring class were not disloyal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe concrete actions (helping land troops, removing rebel flags, public conduct) as indicators of local loyalty rather than only relying on printed proclamations or elite opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade regulation after capture: permits, restrictions, and corruption risk
rubrics_metrics.description: After capture 'Army and Treasury regulations were soon established, and many restrictions placed upon traffic,' but these 'served to throw the trade into a few hands, and thus open the way for much favoritism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impose controls to regulate commerce after occupation, but design permit systems to minimize favoritism and corruption; recognize that too-rapid opening of trade can create inequality and illicit supply lines to the enemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reopening trade until enemy supply is suppressed
rubrics_metrics.description: General Grant and other officers 'made a strong opposition to our policy, and advised the suppression of the Rebellion prior to the opening of trade' because otherwise 'we chastised the Rebels with one hand, while we fed and clothed them with the other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize military objectives over immediate commercial reopening; delay resumption of open trade when it would materially aid hostile forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing transfer of military-relevant goods to the enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Items such as 'boots and shoes ... cloth, clothing, percussion-caps, and similar articles' passed through lines to the Rebels, aiding their forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and restrict movement of goods that can directly equip or sustain enemy forces (footwear, clothing, ammunition components); enforce strict controls and inspections on permitted cargoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' placement and conduct to report battles
rubrics_metrics.description: Press correspondents 'occupied various positions during the engagement'—on tug, in pilot-house, on captured steamer, on transport which was the 'general rendezvous of the journalists.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For effective war reporting secure diverse vantage points (flag-ship, pilot-house, captured craft, reserve transports) and coordinate to obtain full views; be mindful of vessel readiness (e.g., risk if steamer lacks steam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal, respectful communications in demands for surrender
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag-Officer Davis sent a polite formal note requesting surrender; the mayor's reply noted 'the city is in your hands' phrased as falling 'by the force of circumstances'—a 'fine point of law and honor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal respectful language when demanding surrender to preserve legal and honorific considerations for both sides; allow civic authorities face-saving phrasing where appropriate to ease occupation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices for covert dispatch and reconnaissance missions
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonel Ellet's perilous trip: 'took only a few documents to prove his identity,' 'started a little before daylight,' 'waded through swamps,' was 'fired upon by a Rebel picket,' 'concealed dispatches ... in the lining of his boots and in the wristbands of his shirt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For clandestine missions minimize carried documents, travel under cover of darkness, use terrain for concealment, avoid predictable routes, conceal sensitive dispatches on person, and arrange an escort as far as is safe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate naval bombardment with land forces and assess terrain/hydraulics
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to take Vicksburg failed because many Rebel guns were 'located at such a height that it was found impossible to elevate our own guns so as to reach them,' and the canal plan failed because 'the water fell as fast as the digging progressed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before planning river or coastal assaults, assess artillery elevation capabilities relative to enemy battery positions, ensure adequate land forces to occupy captured positions, and evaluate topography and water levels for engineering schemes (canals) to avoid impracticable plans.
